title: Brain Burn
text:
The apartment was wrong before he crossed the threshold.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stood in the doorway of 2E with the rain still on his jacket, reading the air the way the ungoverned lattice had taught him—current direction, dust particle distribution, the minute temperature variance between the space near the window and the space near the door. Someone had been here. Recently. Within the last three hours.

They had opened the window and left it half an inch ajar.

A deliberate tell. A message: *Come and find what we left.*

His hand moved without permission from his conscious mind. The neuretics fired autonomic, and his fingers found the saya at his back before he'd consciously decided to draw. This was what happened when you carried blades for eleven years and let them become a grammar your body spoke without translation. The body got opinions. The body got faster than thought.

He pulled <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> clear. The blade caught the city light bleeding through that half-open window—a thin silver line, steady, reflecting nothing but the fact of itself.

The room was still empty.

He moved to the desk first. The terminal was dark, no intrusion signature, no relay logs corrupted or queued. Whatever they'd done, they hadn't touched the hardware. That meant they wanted him to know they'd *been* here without wanting him to know *what* they'd looked at. Psychological operation. Fear without information. Fear was cheaper than knowledge.

The drawer opened with his left hand. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> still live in his right.

The plate cover was gone.

Not knocked aside. Not disturbed. Gone. And in its place, centered precisely on the drawer's bottom, was a single item: a photograph printed on actual paper—the kind of deliberate, expensive choice that meant *this is important enough to leave physical evidence.*

The image showed his alley. His bike. His window.

And standing in front of it, one hand raised in a small, precise wave, was a figure in a brown coat. The face was obscured by rain and angle, but the posture was familiar in a way that made his spine register it before his mind could process the familiarity.

The woman from the corridor. The one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had said was Marisol.

His hand trembled.

Not fear. Not yet. The tremor came from somewhere deeper—from the recognition that the city had just drawn a line he couldn't uncross. They had walked into his space. They had taken the one thing he'd decided to keep. They had left him proof that they knew exactly where to find him, exactly what mattered, and that the game had moved into a register where the rules had changed.

The apartment was still empty. The window was still open. The rain still fell on the lake twelve kilometers east.

But something in him had slipped a half-step out of sequence—the way it did when the body kept time and the mind didn't. The way it had felt, years back, in the <entity repo="corponation" guid="9aa2545c-d7d5-400c-a3da-b25e2f188dab">DataEast</entity> clinic where nothing was ever what it looked like and the walls had been closer than they seemed.

His phone buzzed.

Not the terminal. The civilian unit. The one that nobody had the number for except three people in the entire city.

The text read: *where are you?*

Raw. No punctuation. No protocol.

He typed back: *home* — which was both true and a lie, because nothing in this apartment felt like home anymore.

The response came fast enough that she must have been waiting: *don't be. coming to you. five minutes. don't answer the door until i text.*

He looked at the photograph on the desk. At the window, still half-open. At his own hand, still trembling around the grip of <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>.

Then he looked at the terminal.

The entity had gone quiet the moment he'd agreed to the Season Two contract. No relay pings. No amendments. No presence at all—just the silence that comes after a commitment is signed and both parties are now waiting to see if either one meant it.

But the entity *knew*. It had to know. The intrusion, the theft, the photograph—these were not random city noise. These were dominoes, each one positioned exactly where it needed to be.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> walked to the window and pushed it fully closed. Locked it. Then he moved to his door and killed the lights, standing in the dark with <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> across his back and the photograph on his desk and the knowledge that something had fundamentally shifted in the eleven-year contract.

The entity had kept him alive all this time.

Now it seemed like someone else was collecting.

And <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, for the first time since he'd walked away from the facility, had no idea which side he was already on.

---

The five minutes stretched. He stood in the dark apartment and counted: the rain on the building's skin, the hum of the thrumline two blocks east where the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> ran through its tunnel, the small electric tick of the terminal cycling through its sleep states. Normal city sounds. All of them suddenly conspicuous, the way a room's silence becomes loudest right before someone enters it.

His phone buzzed twice. The first text was just a single emoji—a door. The second, fifteen seconds later: *moving*.

He opened the door without checking the peephole. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was already there, rain-dark, moving like something with a trajectory and no interest in apology. She had the soldering iron in her hand—not drawn, just present—and her eyes were doing the thing they did when she'd read a system and found it asking the wrong questions.

"Show me," she said.

He stepped back. She came through without touching anything, scanning the room the way she scanned a rig: entry point, exit point, anything that didn't match the baseline. Her eyes landed on the desk, on the photograph, and she stopped moving.

The silence that followed was the kind that has weight.

"How long?" she asked.

"Don't know. The temperature variance puts it between two and four hours. They left the window open a half-inch on purpose."

"They took the plate cover."

"Yeah."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> picked up the photograph without glancing at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, turned it over—blank back, just the image—and set it down again exactly where it had been. Not a gesture of respect. A gesture of someone cataloging evidence. "The woman in the brown coat. The one you said you didn't recognize."

"Same posture. Same coat. But the timestamp doesn't match the corridor sighting."

"Unless there are two of her." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> moved to the window, checked the lock, checked the frame. "This lock is security-grade. She didn't break it. She had the key sequence or she had the credentials to kill the alarm long enough to cycle it manually."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't answer. The hardware in his skull was already running the arithmetic: who had his key sequence, who had his door credentials, who had the level of operational access required to walk into a Tier-2 residential unit, take a specific object, leave a photograph, and walk out again without triggering a single alarm.

The answer was: the entity. And <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity>. And whoever <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> answered to.

"The plate cover." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> turned from the window. "What was in it?"

"Nothing. It was empty. I checked months ago."

She nodded once, like that had answered something larger than the question. "Okay. Pack a bag. Essentials only. We're not coming back here tonight."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>—"

"Not a discussion." She was already moving to his closet, pulling out the small pack he kept ready. The one he'd learned to keep ready, because the city had a way of deciding when you needed to move and not asking first. "They want you scared. They want you thinking about this room, about what they took, about how they got in. While you're standing here counting dust particles, they're doing something else. So we leave. We move. We stop giving them a target to aim at."

She threw the pack on the bed. Started pulling clothes from the drawer—not random, methodical. Three shirts. Two pairs of pants. The spare socks. The things a person needed to stay operational for forty-eight hours without returning home.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched her work. Watched her not look at the photograph again, even though he could feel her reading it anyway, storing the details in whatever system she kept for threats that came through bedroom windows.

"Where?" he asked.

"Not yet. First, we go downstairs. We tell <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-c285-793e-bf21-a84522c9cf94">Auntie</entity> Hoa that your heat's broken and you're staying somewhere else for a few nights. We make it normal. We make it the kind of thing neighbors say and forget."

"And then?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stopped. Turned. Met his eyes for the first time since she'd entered the apartment.

"And then we figure out who's got the key to your door and why they wanted you to know they were here. Because that's not a threat, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. That's an introduction. That's someone saying *I can reach you anywhere you think you're safe.*" She zipped the pack. <entity repo="entertainment" guid="81b4e6d0-c2f9-a37e-5d1b-8c4f0a7e3d92">Handed</entity> it to him. "So we find out who they are. And then we decide what that costs."

He took the pack. The weight of it was familiar—a thing he'd learned long ago, before the entity, before the contracts, back when moving quickly was the only form of survival he knew. But the weight felt different now. Heavier, maybe. Or maybe just real in a way it hadn't been when he'd thought the entity was the only one keeping the books.

The Season Two contract sat in his pocket like a promise he'd made to something that had spent eleven years alone.

Now someone else had walked into his home and left proof they could do it again.

"The photograph," he said. "The woman in the coat. If there are two of her—"

"Then someone's running parallel operations and didn't tell <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> about it. Or <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Able</entity> didn't tell you." <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> moved to the terminal, powered it down manually—the hard kill, no shutdown sequence. "Either way, we're out of this room before they come back to see if the message landed."

She was right. Of course she was right. The photograph wasn't a warning. It was a calling card. And calling cards meant the person holding it was planning to visit again.

He shouldered the pack. Took one last look at the drawer, at the desk, at the window that was no longer quite closed the way he'd left it.

Then he followed <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> into the hallway, where the lights were warm and the building hummed with the ordinary lives of people who didn't know that someone had just rewritten the rules of what safe meant.

Behind them, the apartment waited. Empty. Violated. Keeping its secrets the way violated spaces do—which is to say, not at all. The photograph remained on the desk. The window remained half-closed. The plate cover remained gone.

And in the hallway, moving toward the stairs with a pack on his back and the Season Two contract burning like a promise in his pocket, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt something shift in the architecture of his own survival.

The entity had kept him alive for eleven years.

But it had never kept him safe.

And now someone else had the key.

title: Brain Burn
text:
He works it the way he'd work a scene.

<entity repo="place" guid="945a26fc-6969-5a5b-2737-31fad141a25c">Atlas</entity> NeoCortex hardware — the ungoverned variant, the unit <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> doesn't sell — installed in a brain-burnt nervous system. That's not a modification. A modification needs a base. You modify a wall by adding a door. What <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> had was a nervous system with nothing in it — a <entity repo="corponation" guid="9aa2545c-d7d5-400c-a3da-b25e2f188dab">DataEast</entity> sim junkie scoured down to nothing, the kind of Simulated Reality overdose that empties a mind and leaves the body breathing — and they put software in the empty space.

That's construction.

He knows the ungoverned lattice bone-deep. Eleven years working with it. He knows how the splices carry the load when he runs hot — sixty-four of them, spreading what an ungoverned system won't regulate, buying him time at the cost of heat behind the eyes. He knows the slow damage. He knows the mesh sits in him differently than governed hardware sits in anyone else. He'd always known the ungoverned variant was different. He'd thought that was the hardware's design.

He hadn't thought it was the design working exactly as intended.

He looks at his hands.

Left palm: a knife scar from year three, a job in the North Reclamation that went wrong at the extraction point. Left index: a pressure callus from how he holds <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>, built up over eleven years until it's just part of the hand. Inside the right wrist: a small burn from a welding accident in year seven that he never got around to asking <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> to look at, which she'd probably noticed and chosen not to mention.

Eleven years. Everything in this record is his.

The question "who was I before?" is the wrong question. There is no before. The before was emptied out before the install.

The body is a container. The software is his name.

He sits with that. It doesn't collapse. Eleven years of work it wasn't supposed to survive, and it's still here — carrying <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> and a record of consequences no one else shares. In any way that matters on a job: reliable.

He doesn't know if reliable is enough.

He opens that question and lets it sit.

title: Brain Burn
text:
He tries to reconstruct the escape.

Eleven years ago. <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity>'s facility — he doesn't know where; location as control was the first operational principle, the unknown location as containment. He was inside it. And then he wasn't. That's all he has.

He'd always treated the gap as damage. As something the <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> process did to egress memory — blanking the route as a security measure. Plausible. Filed as plausible.

He runs the gap against what he knows about how the entity works.

He knows the signature. He's been living inside it for eleven years. Doors that open at the wrong moment. Guards with a rotation that doesn't match the schedule. Surveillance with a four-minute gap it didn't have last week. Maybe the entity doesn't manufacture these events. Maybe it reads the sequence from somewhere the dominoes haven't fallen yet, and positions <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> at the right point when they do. If that's true, the coincidences are real. They've been arranged. He can't rule out the plainer read either — patient surveillance, nothing stranger than that.

He runs the gap.

He can't see the content. The memory is empty and it's going to stay empty — he's not going to get content back from a blank that was designed to be blank. Not a blur, not a fade. A seam. What he can see is the shape. He was inside a facility that <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> built to contain exactly what he was. <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> is competent. It built nine <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> subjects before him. It understood the architecture. And yet he got out.

Through a gap.

A gap the entity could have read, somehow, from outside it.

A gap the entity could have arranged to open at the precise moment the program needed the subject in the field.

He stops there. He has to stop. The evidence doesn't go further without him deciding what he wants it to say, and deciding what you want the evidence to say is the one thing that gets operatives killed. He doesn't know if he escaped. He can't know. The memory is gone, and the gap is exactly the shape of the entity's kind of coincidence, and he ended up in the entity's routing network three weeks after his last confirmed <entity repo="corponation" guid="34e17863-d822-4bed-a972-3649099b2444">Praxis</entity> contact.

Three weeks.

He didn't find the entity. The entity found him.

That's not proof. That's a data point in a system he can't fully audit from inside. The escape may have been the final install — the belief in self-determination, indistinguishable from the real thing, because a deployed weapon with authentic conviction performs better than one that knows it's deployed. A clean edit. A section flagged and archived, so the subject carries the conviction of freedom while something else holds the leash. He can't rule it out. The accounting doesn't let him rule it out.

He lets both readings sit open.

Escaped. Deployed. He doesn't close either file. Both fit the record. Both fit the hardware. Both fit the way the entity moves — patient, keeping him alive through <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa5-786f-979b-866522275bbe">E.L.F.</entity>s and bleeds and contracts that should have killed him. The gap doesn't close under either. It just gets wider the longer he looks at it, until he can't see the other side.

The not-knowing is what he has to carry to 35th and Halsted.

He's carried heavier.

title: Brain Burn
text:
He pulls up what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity> said.

Not the whole conversation — the phrase. She'd used it the way she used most things: accurately, without softening, like someone who'd stopped believing a gentled diagnosis was a service to the patient. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aac5-7481-87e1-f66d7a623eb0">Meatbag</entity> haunted by ghosts.

He'd taken it as description. Filed it and moved on.

He opens it now.

Ghosts: sixty-four practitioners, all dead. The <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6ce-ad71-7f25-a057-8e947a52b9eb">Marrow</entity> program archived its contributors permanently — their pattern signatures, their domain responses, the specific shape of how each one solved a problem under pressure. The committee ran the contributions through an averaging process and distilled them into the Persona stack. That stack is still running. Under his name. In the thing that calls itself <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>, in the thing that holds <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and pays <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> exact and is sitting at a dark terminal at whatever hour this is doing the most careful accounting of its life.

The practitioners are dead. Their work is not.

<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aac5-7481-87e1-f66d7a623eb0">Meatbag</entity>: the body the program runs on. A vacated nervous system, chosen for its 64-splice stability profile, for its capacity to hold a parliament under load without the mesh burning out. Selected because it had no resistance to give. The specific body the entity needed, maybe, if this body's architecture really is the only kind built to survive whatever the entity actually is, and if eleven years is how long it's been building toward that.

The full taxonomy: meatbag haunted by ghosts.

He files it.

Not as grief — grief is not in the composite, or if it is, it was placed where it doesn't interfere with function. He files it as taxonomy. As a correct label for the configuration in this chair. The ghosts are real people whose work is running in him without their knowledge or consent, and the meatbag is real, and the haunting is the specific name for the relationship between them.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Nadia</entity>'s description is accurate. He keeps accurate descriptions.

Outside the window, something is happening seventeen floors down on the access apron — a work crew, three people in high-vis mesh, doing something to the structural lamp housing in the methodical way of people who have done it four hundred times. One of them is eating something out of a wrapper. None of them look up.

He moves on to the next line of the accounting.

He sits with the terminal dark for a long time.

The facts: he is a construction. The escape may have been a deployment. He has run the entity's contracts for eleven years, and those contracts built him into the exact instrument the entity needed. He carries sixty-four practitioners' best work, a stranger's emptied nervous system, and an Atlas NeoCortex that is slowly burning through its host. He can't prove he's a person. He's gone over all of it. There's no proof at the end.

What there is, is a position.

He is here. In this chair, in this room, on the thirty-second floor, with <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> across the hall. He can hear her — the small sound of something set down on the workbench, the hum she makes when she's concentrating that she doesn't know she makes. He's known that sound for four years.

The relay is live. The entity has one item in the queue — no scope, no fee, no addendum, no contract number. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> reads it twice; the second read doesn't change it. No sponsor tag, no routing vector, no relay-house signature. The trace runs through the same dead-drop network that's fed him work for eleven years and resolves into nothing, the way it always does, built to be opaque from the inside. Just an address and two words. 35th and Halsted. Bring the sword.

He's going to go.

That's not in question. But he sits with what goes.

He's been in this city eleven years. In this room. That alley. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s stall. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s vault with the old tech and the silence. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s workbench, with its organized mess and the light she keeps on late. He's been in all of those places as this body, with this record. The things that happened, happened to him. No one else was there.

He can't prove the choosing was his and not the last layer of the install. He can't audit himself from the inside. Going over it again won't settle it.

Here's what he can name, and it's true right now: the practitioners are dead. The code they wrote is archived. Whatever is sitting in this chair asking these questions is not dead, not archived, and not a fabrication.

That's not reassurance. It's a starting point.

He stands up. The chair creaks under the shift of weight — salvage, older than the building, with opinions about how a man distributes himself.

He reaches for <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> where it sits sheathed on the table — not to draw it, just the grip, the worn leather, the exact weight that knows his hand by now. The tsukaito cord is worn smooth where eleven years of carrying it has pressed a groove that fits nothing but him. He holds it a moment.

The thing going to 35th and Halsted is not the composite, not the meatbag, not the ghosts. It's the specific, unrepeatable one that has been in every room this record is made of. The code is installed. The response is his.

Reliable is not certainty. Reliable is what you have when certainty isn't on offer.

That's enough to go on.

He clips <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> clipped. He leaves the terminal dark.
